docs.text: Paleofuturistic Python The Python development workflow your past self had always hoped for is finally here. This is a copier template that generates a fully scaffolded, enterprise-ready Python package — uv-managed, ruff-formatted, pytest-tested, properdocs-documented, with vendored CI tooling and a CycloneDX SBOM shipped inside every wheel. The documentation is split by what you're here to do; each area is organized around the Diátaxis framework. The navigation bar at the top is the full map — open an area's dropdown and click a quadrant to unfold its pages. (The panel on the left is just the current page's table of contents.) Using the template You want to generate a Python project and pick the right knobs while doing so. Start with Generate your first project , then From zero to a published package . The Copier questions reference covers every knob. Once your project exists, its own docs ship with it : the scaffold manual (daily workflow, extending tasks, design rationale) lives in the generated docs' Developer section — run ./workflow.cmd document inside your project. Maintaining the template You want to change what this template generates. Start with Make your first template change for the edit-test loop, Test the template for the four test entry points, and Design principles for the constraints every change should respect. The decision records hold the dated history behind those constraints, and a change that settles a new question adds one.

docs.text: ADR-0001: Copier is the delivery mechanism Status : accepted Date : 2026-05-29 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context The template started in November 2024 as a cookiecutter project, with cruft added for updates. Three things kept costing work: Leaving out the unchosen host's files meant a post-generation hook that walked the output and deleted them. A rendering decision was being made as a filesystem operation after the fact. The questionnaire knew strings and lists. Booleans, choices and validation lived in hook code. The vendored _CI/lib/ tree must never be rendered, which cookiecutter expressed as a _copy_without_render glob list that had to be kept in step with the tree. Updates through cruft worked, but cruft tracks the template at the file level with a plain diff, and the hook-driven deletions did not replay cleanly. Decision Migrate the engine to copier . Specifically: copier.yml holds the questionnaire, with typed questions and per-question validator expressions that abort before any file is written. A file or directory whose rendered name is empty is not created, so host- and feature-specific files are expressed as conditional filenames ( {% if git_hosting_service == 'github' %}.github{% endif %} ). Nothing is deleted after generation. Only files ending in .jinja are rendered; everything else is copied verbatim. The vendored tree needs no exclusion list. .copier-answers.yml records the template revision and the answers, and copier update performs a three-way merge against them. The work that cannot be declarative (installing the licence, stamping dates and the uv pin, the executable bit) runs once from tasks_render.py , gated to copier copy . Consequences A generated project has exactly one host code path; from .{{ git_hosting_service }} import … is rendered concrete at copy time and the other module never ships. Generation needs --trust , because the template runs a task. Ownership is per file. Copier cannot know that one section of pyproject.toml is the template's and another the project's, so template-owned files are shaped so that user edits land in predictable places, and project-owned tasks got a file of their own (ADR-0015). A project tracks one template; composing several is not possible. References Commit 115d161 , "migrate the template engine from cruft to copier". Why copier? , Generation internals .

docs.text: ADR-0002: uv is the only tool you install Status : accepted Date : 2025-03-17 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context The lineage this template forked from asked a new contributor for a system Python, pipx, virtualenv, pipenv and pip-tools, and later revisions of this template still had tox, pre-commit and commitizen installed separately. Each tool had its own configuration surface, cache and update cadence, and a fresh checkout was a sequence of installs before the first command worked. Decision uv does every Python operation: it fetches interpreters, creates and syncs the virtualenv, resolves and writes the lockfile, runs every tool through uv run , builds with uv_build , publishes with uv publish , and runs copier itself through uvx . Everything that used to be installed separately is a dependency group inside the project (ADR-0005). The uv version is an exact [tool.uv] required-version pin, so every machine and every job runs the same resolver. uv arrived in March 2025; the last separate install, pipx, left the documentation in October 2025. Consequences One configuration surface: pyproject.toml and uv.lock . No requirements files, no Pipfile. The template is bound to uv's lifecycle. uv is pre-1.0, so a minor release may change behaviour, which is why bump-uv says so loudly when a bump crosses a minor (ADR-0008). An exact pin that lags does not merely age, it refuses to run. That is the reason the pin is stamped fresh at generation rather than inherited from the template (ADR-0008). twine remains only for twine check ; uv does the upload. pyproject.toml stays valid against PEP 517, 518 and 621, so any compliant backend could build it if uv had to be replaced. The migration cost would be one template revision and a copier update . References How uv is used . Design principles: uv is the only tool you install .

docs.text: ADR-0003: Vendored Invoke behind one launcher Status : accepted Date : 2026-03-30, vendoring moved upstream 2026-08-07 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Every development action needed one entry point that works on a fresh clone. The candidates: make is universal but whitespace-sensitive and awkward from Python; just is a binary to install; nox has to be installed before it can install anything. Invoke is Python-native and composable, but installing it first would contradict ADR-0002. Decision Invoke and its dependencies are committed under _CI/lib/vendor/ , and one launcher, workflow.cmd , runs it: a three-line polyglot that sh and Windows cmd both read, each executing uv run python _CI/lib/vendor/bin/invoke --search-root _CI . Tasks live in _CI/tasks/ as Invoke collections. The vendored tree is not maintained here. Since August 2026 it is built by schubergphilis/vendored_invoke , pinned in [tool.vendored-invoke] by tag and by the commit the tag points at, and copied in verbatim by maintain.sync-vendor into both this repository's _CI/lib/ and the template's. Two hand-maintained patches travel with it: one puts the search root on sys.path so nothing is installed, one hard-codes Invoke's version string, which a vendored copy cannot read from package metadata. Consequences ./workflow.cmd works with only uv present, on day one and on day one thousand, and the same Invoke runs on every contributor machine and in CI. The cost is bytes in the repository, and a tree nobody may hand-edit. maintain.sync-vendor refuses a dirty working tree so that the diff it produces is the vendored change alone, and an invariant checks the two trees are byte-identical. The vendored packages ship as source with no .dist-info , so the dependency audit names them from vendor.txt and a hand-edited file is watched by CI rather than audited. _CI/lib is excluded from ruff, and ty gets it as an extra path. References Commits 6a216d1 (vendored tree tracked), 413f883 ( workflow.cmd for Windows), 0ccef7d (upstream vendoring). The _CI tasks architecture , Refresh the vendored invoke .

docs.text: ADR-0004: Pipelines run template commands only Status : accepted Date : 2026-07-28 (practice since 2026-03-30) Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context A workflow file that carries its own uv … , pip install … or properdocs … lines is a second implementation of the development cycle: it drifts from what a developer runs, a failing step cannot be reproduced by typing one command, and the dependencies of a GitHub Action are hidden inside a uses: reference where neither uv.lock nor the SBOM sees them. Decision Every CI step is a ./workflow.cmd <task> call. Behaviour lives in _CI/tasks/ ; the workflow files are glue. Three actions are the whole exception list: actions/checkout , astral-sh/setup-uv where the deps image is not in use, and actions/attest-build-provenance , since only GitHub can record GitHub's provenance attestation. Concretely, docs deploy through properdocs gh-deploy rather than the Pages actions, and tests run through ./workflow.cmd test rather than an inline pytest . One pipeline job cannot follow the rule: GitLab's deps-image job runs in the kaniko image, which has no Python, so it repeats in shell what container.publish does, and an invariant keeps the two tag computations identical. Consequences Parity. The pre-push hook and the CI job run the same ./workflow.cmd preflight , character for character (ADR-0009), so reproducing a pipeline failure means typing what the log shows. Every Python dependency a job uses is pinned in uv.lock and listed in the SBOM. The Pages deploy goes through the legacy branch flow, which GitHub's own internal pipeline then builds; its Node deprecation warning is accepted as the price of keeping deploy logic in document.py . The GitLab shell duplicate is a standing exception, and a candidate for computing the tag in a Python job and handing it to kaniko. References Commit 8aaea04 (workflow test task and CI scaffolding), 5531689 (the principle stated). Design principles: Pipelines run template commands only , Publish docs to GitHub Pages .

docs.text: ADR-0005: Dependency groups, not extras Status : accepted Date : 2025-09-10 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Development tooling used to sit under [project.optional-dependencies] . Extras are a feature of the published package: pip install pkg[lint] is a real command a user can run, and the lint toolchain is not a feature of the library. The docs had to explain that these extras were not really optional, they were internal grouping. Decision Development tooling lives in PEP 735 dependency groups , one group per task family ( build , develop , document , lint , quality , security , test ), with dev as an aggregator of include-group entries. uv run syncs them on demand; lint.pyproject validates the table against the dependency-groups specification, including that every include-group resolves. Consequences Nothing in a group ever reaches the wheel or is user-installable. A package goes in the group whose task runs it. uv run installs every group into one .venv regardless, but the SBOM scopes dev groups as optional , and the audit and a reader of pyproject.toml take the groups at their word. The deps image syncs every group ( uv sync --all-extras --dev ), so CI jobs install nothing. References Commit d79c66b . The Dependency groups reference in the generated-project developer docs, Design principles: Why groups, not extras .

docs.text: ADR-0006: Deliberate non-goals Status : accepted Date : 2026-07-28; the 3.11 floor on 2026-10-26 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context A scaffold that tries to be a framework starter, a service template and a monorepo layout at once ends up with switches for each and tests for every combination. The template's job is one publishable Python package with a complete development cycle around it. Decision Four things the template does not do: No framework choice. It generates a library. FastAPI, Django, Click and the rest are dependencies a project adds. No monorepo support. One package, one repository. No Python below the chosen minimum, which is at least 3.11. Python 3.10 was supported from July 2026 and dropped again in October 2026, so that tomllib is always in the standard library and the tomli fallback could go. No host-specific assumptions in the development cycle. GitHub and GitLab differ only in _CI/tasks/<host>.py and the pipeline file; every other task runs identically. Consequences The questionnaire stays short, and the test matrix stays at two knobs (host and Pages) plus one matured cell. Variants that need a different package shape are a different template, not a question here. Any new host-specific behaviour has to fit the contract both host modules expose; it cannot leak into the shared tasks. References Commits 5531689 (stated), 490daa5 (3.10 added), 059eb2c (3.10 dropped), 71878fb (tomli fallback removed). Design principles: What we deliberately do not do .

docs.text: ADR-0007: Diátaxis for both sites, with the rationale pages shipped Status : accepted Date : 2026-07-28 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context The documentation was one walkthrough that mixed "I want to start" with "I want to understand", and it served two audiences at once: people generating projects from the template and people maintaining the template. Generated projects, meanwhile, got docs that linked to this repository's published site for the rationale, which broke offline and pinned every project to a URL the template does not control. Decision Two documentation sites, each organised by Diátaxis : This repository's site has two areas, Using the template and Maintaining the template , each with tutorials, how-to, reference and explanation. A generated project's site has the project's own four sections plus a Developer section documenting the inherited scaffold, so a project's docs stay about the project. Six explanation pages exist twice. The canonical copy lives here; the shipped copy is an adaptation addressing the project developer, opens with a <!-- canonical: … --> marker, and may knob-gate passages with jinja. An invariant checks the marker and that the shipped page's headings are a subset of the canonical page's. Decision records are not shipped; the shipped explanation pages link to them on the published site. Consequences Each new page has a home decided by what the reader needs, and a reader can tell which site they are on by whether the subject is the template or their project. The six pages are synced by hand. Heading drift is caught; prose drift is not, and the 2026-11-11 audit found some. A maintain.sync-docs task that renders the shipped copies from the canonical ones is the open follow-up. The generated task catalog is checked against the registered tasks, and every page in a generated nav must exist, so the shipped docs cannot name a task or page that is gone. docs.text: ADR-0008: Reproducibility by pin Status : accepted Date : 2026-08-03 (quarantine date), 2026-08-04 (uv pin at generation) Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Three things could change what a project resolved to without a commit changing it: [tool.uv] exclude-newer was a rolling "1 week" , so a package published yesterday could enter the resolution today and turn a gate red with nothing in the history to explain it. The uv pin in the template aged between maintainer bumps, and because required-version is an exact match, a stale pin does not lag, it refuses to run. A project generated months after the last bump started on an obstructive uv. The base image for CI is referenced by tag and by digest, and such a reference resolves to the digest. A bumped tag beside a stale digest silently keeps building the old image. Decision Every entry in every dependency group is an exact version, and exclude-newer is a fixed date that bounds the transitive closure. tasks_render.py stamps it with the generation date, so a new project's boundary is current on its first day and frozen from then on. This repository's own boundary is maintained by hand and re-resolved in the same commit. The uv pin is resolved at generation: the newest release that has been public for at least seven days and that uv-build has published too. The committed pin is the offline fallback and the uv this repository's CI installs. TEMPLATE_UV_VERSION forces a version so the template's own tests generate deterministically. The version and the image digest are never written separately. develop.bump-uv moves the four literals in a project's pyproject.toml , re-resolves the digest, and relocks; maintain.bump-uv moves the template's ten values, one digest per supported Python. Either refuses to write a half-bumped file, and both say loudly when a bump crosses a minor version. Consequences A resolution changes only when a commit changes it. Upgrades are deliberate: raise the date, relock, land the date and the pins together. There is no bot and no scheduled bump. Freshness for new projects comes from generation, not from the committed literal. The seven-day cool-down is also what keeps a stamped uv pin resolvable under a quarantine date stamped the same day. Raising the quarantine date is still a three-step manual flow; a develop.refresh-deps task is the open follow-up. References Commits 0ac5998 (fixed quarantine, resolved lockfile at generation), 6cf4733 (uv pin at generation, bump-uv ). Bump the uv pin , How uv is used .

docs.text: ADR-0009: One QA gate Status : accepted Date : 2026-09-02; the rules stated 2026-09-16 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context The commit hook, the push hook, the aggregator tasks and the CI job each kept their own list of checks, and the lists disagreed about what "green" meant. Per-tool hooks had pre-commit partition the staged files and run them concurrently, so one commit got several verdicts about several subsets of itself. Whole-program checks narrowed to the staged files answered wrongly: ty needs the callers of a changed signature, pyscn needs every file to know what is dead, and a wheel builds from the whole tree. And commit latency grew with the project rather than with the change. Decision Every check is declared once, in STEPS in _CI/tasks/preflight.py , with a scope, a path filter and whether it writes a derived file. Three consumers read that registry: preflight.staged , what the commit hook runs: the per-file steps over the staged files, one invocation, one verdict. preflight , what the pre-push hook and the CI job run, character for character: every step over the whole project. The pre-commit configuration's one files: pattern, which an invariant asserts is exactly the union of the registry's filters. Scope decides the tier. A check that answers from the staged files alone runs on every commit; one that needs the whole program runs on push. Steps run cheapest first, every step runs even after one fails, and the derived-file steps are skipped once anything has failed. The only flag that changes what runs is --audit-dependencies , which adds the network step. There is no flag that runs less: env_list is what shortens the matrix, and it shortens CI with it. Consequences Adding a check is one registry entry; it reaches its tier without editing three files. The commit hook stays fast as the project grows; the push hook costs about one suite-length. SKIP=preflight git push is the escape hatch, and CI runs the same command regardless, so a skipped check is deferred, never avoided. The whole-program steps are the same list in the hook name, the CI comment and the docs, and invariants hold those lists to the registry. References Commits 71e37c7 (the registry and preflight ), 715fba3 (the rules written down). Design principles: The QA gate .

docs.text: ADR-0010: Verifying is the default, writing is a flag Status : accepted Date : 2026-09-02 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Tasks used to refresh README badges and the coverage ratchet as a side effect of running. A hook that writes aborts the push having modified files the author never staged, which is what teaches people --no-verify . A CI job cannot commit a refreshed badge anyway. And wherever the verifying side was a second implementation of the generating side, the two drifted and the gate stopped meaning anything. Decision The bare command compares; --write updates. preflight with no flag is the gate the hooks and the pipeline run, so reproducing a failure needs no flag. Every derived value, the four badges and fail_under , is written through one function, apply_badge , with a write parameter. What verifying compares is exactly what writing would have produced. A derived value is written only by the command that measured it: the coverage badge by the matrix run, the pyscn badge by the analysis that produced the grade, the version badge by release.bump . document writes no badge, because building docs is not changing a README. Names decide. A command named for an inspection may not modify the tree; one named for a mutation may, which is why format and release.bump write without being asked. Flags add, never subtract. --write and --audit-dependencies are the only ones the gate takes. Consequences A freshly generated project needs one preflight --write to fill in coverage-unknown and pyscn-not rated , and one more after git remote add origin . A value that cannot be computed at all fails --write too, so "wrote nothing, exited 0" cannot let a stale badge reach the default branch. The CI badge is only half checked: its URL is a fact about the clone's origin , not about the tree, so the gate asks only whether the shipped placeholder survives once a remote exists. References Commit 71e37c7 . Design principles: Who may write what the checks measure .

docs.text: ADR-0011: Report names carry a scope Status : accepted Date : 2026-09-09, after the per-env split of 2026-09-02 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Coverage across a version matrix is a union: a line counts as covered if any interpreter ran it, and version-gated code is covered by no single interpreter. Three bugs came from readers not knowing which scope a file held: Under tox run-parallel , five environments wrote one reports/coverage.json at once, and the badge read whichever finished last, possibly mid-write. test.pytest outside tox wrote the same file with one interpreter's number, overwriting the union the badge and the ratchet had read. fail_under , set by the ratchet from the union, was enforced by pytest-cov per interpreter, and no single interpreter can clear a floor only the union reaches. It took three passes to find every writer. Decision A report's name says what scope produced it, and whatever writes a name must run at that scope: reports/coverage.json means the union across env_list , and is written only by combine_coverage after the whole matrix. reports/coverage.<env>.json is one environment's report; coverage.local.json is whatever a bare pytest happened to use. Nothing reads either. Each environment measures into its own .coverage.<env> data file. fail_under is enforced once, against the union; every other coverage command passes --fail-under=0 , addopts included. test.tox --env=<one> writes under that environment's name and refuses --write , because one interpreter's coverage is not what the badge means. The same rule covers the CI badge: its value is a fact about a clone, so no run is at the right scope to judge it, and it is written but never verified (ADR-0010). Consequences The badge and the ratchet read a filename, not a provenance, and the filename is now enough. coverage erase leaves per-env data alone, so the matrix task deletes .coverage.* and the per-env reports by hand before each run, or a dropped environment would inflate the union. Trimming env_list can lower the measured union and fail the next run. That is the ratchet working. References Commits a706f2e (per-env data and combine), 10011e5 (the local report renamed). Testing strategy , the module docstring of template/_CI/tasks/preflight.py .

docs.text: ADR-0012: The SBOM ships inside the wheel Status : accepted Date : 2026-03-30 (SBOM generated), 2026-05-28 (inside the wheel) Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context A bill of materials produced beside a release has to be correlated with it afterwards: stored somewhere, named after the version, found again when someone asks "are we affected by CVE-X?". The first version of this template generated one with the cyclonedx-bom CLI and uploaded it to a Dependency-Track server, which tied every project to one SCA platform and one set of credentials. Decision _CI/tasks/sbom.py composes a CycloneDX 1.7 SBOM with cyclonedx-python-lib and writes it to src/<package>/sbom.cdx.json . That path is inside the package data tree, so uv build ships it inside the wheel without any packaging configuration. It covers four sources, distinguished by scope: runtime dependencies ( required ), dependency groups ( optional ), the vendored CI tooling ( excluded ) and the chosen host's pipeline components ( excluded ), joined by a two-level dependency graph through a synthetic build-environment component. Each component carries a licence, a lockfile hash where there is one, and a link to its upstream page. The file is validated against the CycloneDX schema and regenerated by secure.sbom as part of every build . Consequences A consumer extracts it with unzip -p <wheel> <package>/sbom.cdx.json or importlib.resources . No separate artefact, no correlation step. The SBOM is a build input, so it is deterministic from the tree, and the dependency audit is deliberately not bundled with it (ADR-0013). Composing it costs about a second of imports, which is why secure.py imports sbom.py lazily and the launcher stays fast for every other task. The SBOM's VCS reference is read from origin , so CI checkouts must leave no credential in the remote URL; the publish job's checkout persists none. Which SCA platform reads the SBOM is the organisation's call. The Dependency-Track upload was removed in November 2026. References Commits d49e369 (first SBOM), 7e6c695 (embedded in the wheel), 1e83250 (Dependency-Track removed). SBOM and security model , Design principles: SBOMs ship inside the wheel .

docs.text: ADR-0013: The audit runs on a schedule and on the dependency surface Status : accepted Date : 2026-09-02, replacing the every-gate run of 2026-08-03 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context A dependency audit's answer depends on the advisory database on the day it runs, not on the branch. Three placements were tried or considered, and each had a failure mode: Reachable only as a local command, the audit gated nothing, and the expiry dates in .security-overrides never came due because nothing ran on the day they passed. In every automated gate, as it was from August 2026, a docstring change went red for a CVE published overnight that its author neither introduced nor could fix, which is the kind of noise that teaches people to ignore a red pipeline. Inside build , a fresh advisory made it impossible to build a wheel from code that had built the day before, blocking a hotfix on an unrelated finding. Decision The audit is triggered on the two axes it varies along: Time. A daily schedule on GitHub ( cron , off the hour), and a schedule pipeline rule on GitLab. This is what makes the expiry dates load-bearing. The dependency surface. A push that touches uv.lock , _CI/lib/vendor.txt , the vendored tree or its patches, or .security-overrides . Not pyproject.toml : the project runs --frozen , so an edit that changes what is installed changes the lockfile with it, while a ratchet bump or a version bump does not fire a full audit of an untouched dependency set. Publishing is gated separately: release.dist audits before it builds, because that is the moment the outside world is exposed. preflight --audit-dependencies adds the step locally; the bare gate never runs it. In this repository's own matrix the audit rides with the matured cell only, so a transient advisory-service error fails one job instead of five. Consequences A pull request from a fork triggers no audit; the scheduled run after the merge covers it. A hand-edited vendored file is watched, not audited: no scanner can read a patched source, so the push fires the job to put the diff in front of a human. secure remains the human-facing aggregator; nothing automated calls it. References Commits 839734b (audit in every gate), 0b871d3 (separated from the build, narrowed to schedule and surface). SBOM and security model: Layer 1 .

docs.text: ADR-0014: A release is the version bump arriving on the default branch Status : accepted Date : 2026-11-11, after the GitLab fix of 2026-11-10 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context ./workflow.cmd release used to create the tag v<version> on the release branch and push it with the branch, and the publish pipeline triggered on tags. Two things went wrong with that: On GitLab the tag push published the version before the merge request had been reviewed. On both hosts a squash or rebase merge left the tag pointing at a commit the default branch never saw, and nothing published. A tag is the wrong signal: it is created before the review and it does not follow the merge. Decision release prepares a release/<version> branch, bumps the version with cz bump --version-files-only , refreshes the version badge in the same commit, writes the changelog, pushes and opens the pull or merge request. It creates no tag. The publish job runs on every push to the default branch and hands the push to release.ship . That reads [project].version at the previous tip and the new one; if it changed, the push carried a release. release.ship then creates the tag on the new tip through the host's Release API, with the token the job already holds ( GITHUB_TOKEN with contents: write , or CI_JOB_TOKEN ), builds, signs the attestations and uploads. With no bump it prints so and exits 0. The Pages workflow asks the same question through release.detect before deploying the docs. Consequences Any merge method publishes, and nothing publishes before review. The pypi environment is protected by restricting it to the default branch, not by required reviewers, which would hold every push. The review that guards a release is the pull request's. A tag ruleset must leave creation unrestricted, since the Actions token creates the tag and no bypass list is guaranteed to accept it. release.push lost its purpose and was removed. A release branch opened before the change carries a tag that has to be deleted before merging. The default branch was spelled main in the tasks, the workflows and the badge URL until ADR-0040 made it a copier answer. References Commits 8287f97 (GitLab publishes only once the tag reaches main), 4e278ff (tag on main from CI), 9f6e054 (tag rulesets). docs.text: ADR-0015: local.py is the project's module Status : accepted Date : 2026-08-03 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Copier ownership is per file (ADR-0001). Every module under _CI/tasks/ is template-owned and replaced on copier update , so a task a project added to lint.py , or a registration it added to __init__.py , collided on every update, forever. Projects needed somewhere to put their own tasks that the template would never reach for. Decision The template seeds _CI/tasks/local.py once, with an empty local namespace and a worked example in its docstring, and lists it in _skip_if_exists so that copier update neither overwrites it nor raises a conflict on it. __init__.py imports it when the file exists, adds its namespace, and gives it the same bootstrap pre-task the built-in namespaces get, so there is no registration step. A missing file is skipped as a deliberate deletion; an error inside it propagates, because silently dropping someone's tasks is worse than a traceback. Consequences Project tasks survive every update; ./workflow.cmd local.<task> works as soon as the task is written. Changing a template task is done by wrapping it from local.py , not by editing it in place. Only local.py itself is protected. Extra modules imported from it are unprotected but never collide, since the template ships no file of those names. References Commit 8d7ec2c , "give projects a task module the template never overwrites". Add a workflow task in the generated-project developer docs, Extend the template workflow tasks .

docs.text: ADR-0016: Ruff replaces Black, isort and flake8; pylint stays for what Ruff lacks Status : accepted Date : 2024-11-18; pylint and complexipy added 2026-03-30 and 2026-04-10 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context The formatter, the import sorter and the linter used to be three tools with three configuration blocks, three caches and three sets of version pins, and they disagreed with each other often enough that a project needed a compatibility section for each pair. Decision Ruff does formatting ( ruff format ), import sorting ( ruff check --select I --fix ) and linting ( ruff check with select = ["ALL"] and a short, commented ignore list). pylint stays for the checks Ruff does not have, and complexipy adds cognitive complexity over src/ . All three are held to one line length, 120, and the same rule set applies to src/ , tests/ and _CI/tasks/ , with _CI/ carrying its own lighter pyproject.toml for the few rules that make no sense in task code. This repository's own tests/ and _CI/ are judged by the same configuration. Consequences One tool, one configuration block, one cache for most of the lint gate; pylint is the slow step and runs last, behind everything cheaper that could also fail. pylint's role is expected to shrink as Ruff grows; nothing is configured twice on purpose. A rule disabled for one line is disabled in code with # noqa , with the reason beside it, not in the configuration. References Commits ac2147c (Ruff), 8aaea04 (pylint in the task set), 86e6c1d (complexipy). Design principles: Ruff replaces Black + isort + flake8 .

docs.text: ADR-0017: ty replaces mypy Status : accepted Date : 2026-03-30 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Type checking was the slowest step in the lint gate, and mypy's configuration surface was the one place the toolchain did not share a vendor with uv and Ruff. docs.text: ADR-0018: pytest replaces unittest, with xdist at a fixed worker count Status : accepted Date : 2024-11-18; -n 4 fixed on 2026-09-08 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context The original lineage ran python -m unittest . Fixtures, parametrisation, coverage integration and parallel execution all needed either boilerplate or a plugin layer unittest does not have. Decision pytest is the runner, with pytest-cov for branch coverage, pytest-xdist for parallel execution, pytest-html for the on-demand report and pytest-env for a .env file. xdist runs a fixed four workers rather than -n auto : under tox run-parallel every environment spawns its own pool, so auto on a sixteen-core machine asked for eighty workers and came out slower than four. Four is chosen for the suite a project will have, not the two tests it ships with. Consequences Unittest-style classes still work; pytest discovers them. On the scaffold's two tests xdist costs more than it saves; the cost starts paying once a suite is large enough to spread. -n 0 is the knob while a suite is tiny. Tests that cannot run in parallel need a marker and a two-pass setup the template does not ship, because most projects do not need it. References Commits 6dbb96f (pytest from the first commit), acb1bf9 (fixed worker count). Testing strategy , Design principles: pytest, not unittest .

docs.text: ADR-0019: Conventional Commits drive the changelog, not the version Status : accepted Date : 2026-04-10 (commit linting), 2026-04-14 (release flow) Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Release notes written by hand are the first thing a release skips. Deriving them from commit messages needs the messages to parse, and a tool that also infers the version bump from the same messages, as Release Please and commitizen's autorelease do, turns a feat: typed in a hurry into a minor release nobody meant. Decision Commit messages follow Conventional Commits , checked by lint.commitizen as a commit-msg hook and over the unpushed range in the gate. commitizen generates the changelog from the commits since the last tag, grouped by type through a change_type_map . The version bump is an explicit choice: ./workflow.cmd release -i <type> , with cz bump --version-files-only writing the version through uv's version provider so pyproject.toml and uv.lock move together. Autorelease is not used. Consequences A commit prefix decides where a line lands in the changelog and nothing else. The lint step rejects a message that does not parse, so the history stays usable as release notes. The changelog is incremental and lives on the docs page the nav shows (ADR-0031). References Commits 6f2f433 (commit-message linting), d0a2880 (release flow with cz bump ). Design principles: Conventional Commits drive the release notes .

docs.text: ADR-0021: Trusted Publishing with PEP 740 attestations by default Status : accepted Date : 2026-11-10 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Publishing with a long-lived PyPI API token stored as a CI secret means a leaked secret can publish anything, and a wheel on PyPI says nothing about which pipeline built it. PyPI accepts PEP 740 attestations only from a Trusted Publisher, so provenance and the credential model are one decision. Decision The publish job authenticates to PyPI with the host's OIDC token: id-token: write on GitHub, id_tokens: with audiences pypi and sigstore on GitLab. release.attest signs an attestation per wheel and sdist with that identity, uv publish --trusted-publishing always uploads the files with their attestations, and on GitHub actions/attest-build-provenance records a second attestation with the repository. The pypi environment is restricted to the default branch, not to reviewers. UV_PUBLISH_* credentials switch the whole path: when all three are set the upload uses them with --no-attestations and release.attest signs nothing, because an index without Trusted Publishing may reject an upload that carries attestations. Empty values are dropped first, since GitHub injects an undefined secret as an empty string and uv reads an empty UV_PUBLISH_URL as a URL. Consequences No PyPI secret exists anywhere; PyPI's Trusted Publisher form is a one-time setup per project. On GitLab, Trusted Publishing works from gitlab.com only; a self-managed instance uses the credential path. Nothing rebuilds between attesting and uploading (ADR-0014), or the attestation would name files that were never published. References Commit b1a48da , "cover every PyPA packaging specification". SBOM and security model: Layer 3 , Harden the GitHub repository .

docs.text: ADR-0022: One commit-stage hook, and no files: filter on pre-push Status : accepted Date : 2026-09-02 (one hook), 2026-09-08 (no filter on pre-push) Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Five pre-commit hooks, one per tool, had pre-commit partition the staged files and run the tools concurrently: five banners, five reads of the index, five verdicts about five subsets of one commit. Separately, a files: filter on the pre-push hook meant a push carrying only README.md and pyproject.toml , which is exactly what the recovery loop produces after preflight --write , skipped the gate on the very push meant to prove it green, while CI still ran it in full. Decision The commit stage is one hook running ./workflow.cmd preflight.staged , with pass_filenames: false because the task reads the index itself. The hook's files: pattern decides only whether it wakes, and an invariant asserts it is exactly the union of the registry's per-step filters. The pre-push hook runs ./workflow.cmd preflight with no files: filter and no flag, so it is the command the pipeline runs and nothing can pass locally that CI rejects. A third commit-stage hook runs secure.validate-overrides only when .security-overrides is staged. Consequences One verdict per commit, in registry order, cheapest first. Launcher startup is about a tenth of a second, so the argument for one hook is legibility, not the seconds. SKIP=<id> suspends one hook and leaves the others; --no-verify is documented as the thing to avoid. References Commits 71e37c7 ( preflight.staged ), 4e891d3 (filter removed from pre-push). Configuration files: .pre-commit-config.yaml in the generated docs, ADR-0009.

One message that predates the convention, a squashed import, history from before the template was applied, a --no-verify from last year, fails every run from then on, with no way past it except skipping the whole gate. docs.text: ADR-0025: Coverage is a union, fail_under is enforced once, and the ratchet starts dormant Status : accepted Date : 2026-05-29 (dormant ratchet), 2026-09-02 (union) Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context A coverage floor that only moves up keeps coverage from regressing silently, but two things made a naive ratchet unusable. The scaffold's smoke test drives a fresh project to 100% on day one, so a ratchet that engaged immediately locked the bar at 100 and failed the first real change. And a version matrix produces five coverage numbers, none of which is the project's coverage: version-gated code is reached by some interpreters and not others, so each reports a miss on code the matrix as a whole exercises. Decision Coverage across the matrix is the union: coverage combine over the per-environment data files, written once to reports/coverage.json . A line counts as covered if any interpreter ran it. Averaging would be meaningless; coverage is a set of lines, not a noisy measurement. fail_under is enforced once, by the combine, against the union it was measured from. Every other coverage command passes --fail-under=0 . The ratchet is dormant while def test_sanity is still in the scaffolded test file ( [tool.test-ratchet] mode = "auto-detect" ). Removing it engages the ratchet; once any non-zero fail_under is written, dormancy is over for good. mode = "strict" engages it on the first run, for a scaffold seeded into an already-covered codebase. Consequences The bar only goes up; lowering it is a deliberate, reviewable edit in the same commit as the code that needed it. Trimming env_list can lower the union and fail the next run. That is the ratchet working. The template's own matrix needs a matured cell to exercise any of this (ADR-0038). References Commits 9c0f82b (dormant ratchet), a706f2e (combine per-env data). Testing strategy , ADR-0011.

docs.text: ADR-0026: pyscn produces JSON in the gate and HTML on demand Status : accepted Date : 2026-09-04 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Three things about pyscn were discovered the hard way. It opens a browser as soon as it writes an HTML report, which made quality.pyscn-analyze open the report twice and had a tool reaching for a browser on a CI runner. It allows one output format per run, so --html --json fails and each format costs a full analysis with its own summary table. And --quiet , whose help promises to suppress output unless issues are found, suppresses the issues too: a failure reported only "Found 1 quality issue(s)" with no file or line. Decision Every HTML run passes --no-open . Whether a report is worth opening is the task's decision, and is_ci() is part of it. The gate produces JSON only, through pyscn_json_report : the badge reads the grade from it, and nothing in a hook or a pipeline opens an HTML report. quality.pyscn-analyze produces both and opens the HTML, for a human who asked. pyscn check is never --quiet . Two lines on a passing run buy the one line that names the finding on a failing one. analyze and check are both in the gate and are not a duplicate: analyze computes the lenient aggregate grade the badge shows, check applies the hard thresholds that fail the tree. Reports are cleared before each run, since pyscn timestamps them and reports/ would grow for as long as the project runs its gate. Consequences The gate produces what it consumes and nothing else, which is the general rule (ADR-0009). A failed analysis leaves the directory empty, so the badge reports that it has no grade to read rather than certifying one measured against a tree that has since changed. References Commits 1bc1b6e ( --no-open ), a9a78db (JSON only in the gate), cf69fe4 (why not --quiet ). template/_CI/tasks/quality.py .

docs.text: ADR-0027: Heavy imports stay out of launcher startup Status : accepted Date : 2026-05-28 (in-process validation), 2026-09-08 (lazy import) Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Every ./workflow.cmd invocation imports every task module, so a module-scope import in any of them is paid by every task. cyclonedx-python-lib 's JSON validator reaches jsonschema._format and builds a lark grammar at import time: 1.0 second of the 1.2 seconds sbom.py cost to import, paid by ./workflow.cmd lint which never composes an SBOM. Separately, SBOM validation used to run in a uv run python subprocess, because the launcher puts the vendored tree earlier on sys.path than the venv and the vendored tree once carried its own jsonschema , so an in-process import resolved to the wrong copy. That jsonschema was a transitive dependency of the vendoring toolchain, which is no longer vendored. Decision secure.py imports sbom.py inside the three tasks that compose an SBOM, not at module scope, and sbom.py imports the validator inside validate_sbom . With the stray jsonschema gone, validation runs in-process and the subprocess has nothing left to isolate. An invariant asserts no task module imports cyclonedx at module scope. Consequences Launcher startup is about a tenth of a second, which is what makes one commit hook per commit cheap enough to argue for on legibility alone (ADR-0022). The vendored tree must contain nothing but what the shipped _CI/ code imports; the vendor extra in _CI/pyproject.toml is the list, and the upstream build enforces it. docs.text: ADR-0028: The audit reads uv.lock directly and retries a run with no verdict Status : accepted Date : 2026-09-08 (retry), 2026-09-09 (lockfile) Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Two narrower forms of the audit each saw less than the lockfile. pip-audit with no -r enumerates installed distributions, so a Linux runner omitted whatever a platform marker, an extra or an unsynced group kept out of the venv. uv export produces a universal requirements file that keeps the markers, and pip-audit evaluates them, so the same pins were skipped a step later. And a url source matched the string form of the source table and was audited as though a PyPI release of that name existed. Separately, pip-audit walks the advisory database one package at a time with no retry of its own, so a single reset connection failed a run that had established nothing, and the first retry logic keyed on a Python traceback, which would have gone quietly inert the day pip-audit caught the exception and printed a message instead. Decision secure.audit reads [[package]] entries straight out of uv.lock : every version for every interpreter and platform, no markers to evaluate, no groups to remember. Only packages with a registry key in their source table are audited; git, URL and path sources are named on stdout as unauditable rather than dropped silently. One requirement file per version slot, because pip-audit refuses a file naming a package twice and a lockfile legitimately pins two versions behind different markers. _CI/lib/vendor.txt is audited by name, the vendored tree having no .dist-info . --strict , so a package the service cannot resolve fails the audit instead of landing in a skip table under exit 0. A run is retried only while its output contains none of the phrases pip-audit prints when it reached a conclusion either way. A finding is never retried. Three attempts, three then six seconds apart. Consequences Everything written about the audit can claim every locked version. What it still cannot see: a hand-edited vendored file, and [build-system] requires . The retry bias is deliberate: the worst it can do to a genuine finding is nothing. References Commits 8d22ec5 (a reset connection is not a finding), 10011e5 (audit the lockfile), a3d7b9f (a url source is not a registry source). SBOM and security model: Layer 1 .

docs.text: ADR-0029: Suppressions come from three sources, and the two outside the repository must expire Status : accepted Date : 2026-04-22 (the file), 2026-08-03 (validation and required expiry) Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context A pipeline needs to suppress a finding without committing anything, and a person wants the reverse: a suppression that is reviewed with the code and resurfaces on a date. A suppression passed in from outside the repository with no expiry would mute a finding forever with no code change to review. And a scanner that matched id-shaped substrings let a mistyped expiry such as CVE-1::2020-1-1 through as a permanent suppression with the date fragments tacked on as extra ids. Decision Three sources, merged in precedence order and deduplicated by id: secure.audit --ignore , the <PROJECT>_SECURITY_OVERRIDE environment variable, and the .security-overrides file. Every entry is <VULN_ID>[::YYYY-MM-DD] , matched whole, with the justification in a # comment. Entries from the two sources that leave no trace in the repository must carry an expiry. Expired entries are reported and ignored. Whatever is applied is printed with its origin, so a suppression injected through CI configuration still shows in the build log. An expiry further out than a year is remarked on but allowed. secure.validate-overrides checks the file's syntax as a commit hook whenever it is staged. Consequences A permanent suppression has to be in the file, where it shows in a diff. The scheduled audit is what brings an expiry round with nobody pushing (ADR-0013). The template's own matrix forwards its .security-overrides and TEMPLATE_SECURITY_OVERRIDE through the same variable, so the plumbing is exercised. References Commits 0f5c4b1 (the file), 32f6ba8 (validation, required expiry off-repo). Triage a security finding in the generated-project developer docs.

docs.text: ADR-0030: Task commits follow the signing configuration, retried unsigned only on a signing failure Status : accepted Date : 2026-08-04 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context release.bump and release.changelog commit. Hardcoding --no-gpg-sign breaks exactly the repositories that care most about provenance, where a branch rule rejects unsigned commits at push time. Forcing a signature breaks CI, which usually has no signing key, and a release must not stop on a documentation commit. A naive "retry unsigned on any failure" would retry a pre-commit hook failure too, and report a signing problem that does not exist. Decision shared.commit tries a signed commit first, letting git decide from commit.gpgsign . It retries with --no-gpg-sign only when both guards hold: git was asked to sign, and the failure is git's own "failed to write commit object" line, which is how a signing failure surfaces whatever gpg.format is set to. The retry says plainly that the commit is unsigned and what that costs. Consequences A developer with a key gets signed release commits; CI gets unsigned ones with a warning. The cause line above git's summary is format-specific (openpgp and ssh print different things), so the marker is the summary line, verified against both formats on git 2.x. References Commit 6a841e1 , "sign the changelog commit when the repository asks for it". commit and signing_requested in template/_CI/tasks/shared.py .

docs.text: ADR-0033: The deps image is content-addressed over three inputs and handed on by digest Status : accepted Date : 2026-08-03 (image caching from 2026-04-10) Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context CI jobs run inside a prebuilt image holding the project's dependencies, so each job starts warm. The image tag was derived from the lockfile alone, so editing Dockerfile.deps or bumping the base image changed the image's contents without changing its tag, and CI kept running a stale image. Downstream jobs also consumed the tag, which could be repointed between the build job and the job that ran inside it. Decision deps_image_tag() hashes uv.lock , Dockerfile.deps and the resolved base-image reference. Each input is reduced to its own fixed-width digest before being folded into the outer hash, so no combination of inputs can collide with a different combination and the algorithm is reproducible in shell with sha256sum . container.publish resolves the pushed image to repository@sha256:… and writes that to .deps-image , so a tag repointed mid-run cannot change the container a later job runs in. Consequences A change to any of the three inputs produces a new tag; the same three reuse the image. GitLab's pipeline job computes the same tag in shell, and an invariant keeps the two in step (ADR-0035). The base image carries its own digest (ADR-0008), which is one of the three inputs, so a base bump rebuilds rather than serving an image built on the old base. References Commits 4fbd8fc (image caching), 607d850 (content-addressed tag, digest pinning). CI framework internals in the generated-project developer docs.

docs.text: ADR-0034: The deps image runs as uid 1001 Status : accepted Date : 2026-08-03 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Every CI job ran as root inside the deps image. Dropping root is routine hardening, but the uid is not arbitrary: GitHub's hosted runners own the mounted workspace with uid 1001, and a mismatch leaves the checkout unwritable to the job. Decision Dockerfile.deps ends with useradd --uid 1001 , USER 1001 and a home directory. /app is chowned to that user because the image is built with --no-install-project , so uv run installs the project into UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT at job time and needs to write there, and uv needs a writable HOME for its cache. Consequences Nothing in CI runs as root. A runner with a different uid gets permission errors under the checkout; changing the uid in the Dockerfile fixes it and, because the Dockerfile is a tag input (ADR-0033), rebuilds the image rather than serving one built for the old uid. On GitLab the clone is performed by a helper container, so the project directory can arrive root-owned depending on runner configuration; the generated docs say what that looks like. References Commit 2087c73 , "harden generated pipelines and drop root from the deps image". template/Dockerfile.deps .

docs.text: ADR-0035: GitHub reuses an existing deps tag; GitLab's pipeline job builds with kaniko in shell Status : accepted Date : 2026-04-10 (GitHub reuse), 2026-04-20 (kaniko), 2026-11-11 (GitLab task uses docker) Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Building the deps image on every run costs a full image build per gated push. On GitHub the build job can ask ghcr whether the tag already exists and pull it instead. On GitLab, shared runners allow no docker daemon, privileged docker-in-docker or user namespaces, which rules out docker, buildah and podman; kaniko builds in userspace, but its image has no Python or uv, so ./workflow.cmd cannot run there. Decision GitHub. publish_deps_image inspects the manifest and, when the tag exists, pulls it so a repo digest exists locally; otherwise it builds and pushes. Reusing a tag trusts whoever pushed it first, so the mitigation is access control: only the deps job holds packages: write , and the generated docs name the trade-off and how to remove it. GitLab. The pipeline's deps job is the one job that does not go through the launcher. It repeats the tag computation and the push in shell, with kaniko and a Deploy Token scoped to a deps environment, and hands downstream jobs the digest from --digest-file . There is no reuse path, so the image can only ever be what that run produced. container.publish by hand builds the same reference with docker or podman, since November 2026; before that the task ran the kaniko executor, which only exists inside the kaniko image where the task cannot start. Consequences An invariant pins the shell duplicate to the Python tag algorithm. The GitLab duplicate is a standing exception to ADR-0004, and the candidate fix is computing the tag in a Python job and passing it to kaniko as a dotenv artifact. The Deploy Token variables must be Protected, Masked and scoped to the deps environment, or a fork's merge request could read a registry write token. References Commits 4fbd8fc (GitHub reuse), ec87192 (kaniko), 607d850 (the trade-off written down), a668ea0 (GitLab task on docker). Build and push a container and CI framework internals in the generated-project developer docs.

docs.text: ADR-0036: Checkouts persist no credentials Status : accepted Date : 2026-08-03 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context actions/checkout bakes a token into the origin remote ( https://x-access-token:<token>@github.com/owner/repo.git ) and leaves it in .git/config . The SBOM reads origin for its VCS reference and ships inside the wheel, so a token written there would become a permanent public artefact on PyPI. The same applies to the badge URL and to anything else that reads the remote back. Decision Every checkout in the generated workflows sets persist-credentials: false , so auth goes into an http.extraheader that is removed once the fetch is done and origin stays a clean URL. The one exception is the Pages deploy job, which pushes to gh-pages with those credentials and builds no SBOM. As a second line, strip_credentials removes any userinfo from a remote before the SBOM, the badge or the release helpers use it. An invariant asserts none of the checkout copies drifts. Consequences The publish job cannot push, even if a build step were compromised; release.tag creates the tag through the API with the token the job holds instead. The workflow-level permissions: floor is contents: read , with each job widening only what it needs. References Commit 2087c73 . The note above the jobs in continuous-integration.yaml , strip_credentials in template/_CI/tasks/shared.py .

docs.text: ADR-0037: Docs deploy on release through gh-deploy , with an explicit Pages build request Status : accepted Date : 2026-09-07 (on release); build request 2026-07-28; release.detect 2026-11-11 Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context Three things, in order. GitHub's upload-pages-artifact and deploy-pages actions bring dependencies that appear in neither uv.lock nor the SBOM, and deploy logic that lives in YAML. A push made with the Actions GITHUB_TOKEN to the gh-pages branch does not trigger the legacy deploy-from-branch build, so a deploy that pushed and stopped published nothing. And a site deployed on every push to the default branch describes code that is in no release yet, so a reader can reach for something they cannot install. Decision document.deploy-github runs properdocs gh-deploy --force , a Python command from the lockfile, then requests a Pages build through the API. The workflow triggers on a push to the default branch and asks release.detect whether the push carried a release, the same question the publish job asks through release.ship , and deploys from the detected commit. Since November 2026 that detection is the task itself; before, a separate detect-release-tag.yaml did it. workflow_dispatch remains so a project that has not released can publish its docs at all. The deploy job is the one checkout that persists credentials (ADR-0036). Consequences The site and the package cannot disagree about what counts as released. GitHub's own pages-build-deployment pipeline prints a Node deprecation warning that this template cannot silence without adopting the actions it chose not to; the warning is accepted. Versioned docs, a stable and a dev build, would need more machinery than the template ships. References Commits 1e0dd3f (gh-deploy), 3b1efd6 (Pages build request), 38acf6f (on release), 4e278ff ( release.detect ). Publish docs to GitHub Pages .

docs.text: ADR-0038: Template tests generate from a snapshot, pin the uv version, and run one matured cell Status : accepted Date : 2026-04-24 (matrix), 2026-08-04 (pinned uv), 2026-09-08 (matured cell), 2026-11-10 (snapshot) Record written : 2026-11-11 (backfilled) Context The template's own tests generate projects and run their gates. Three things about that needed settling. Copying the whole working tree into the snapshot let caches, .DS_Store files and agent state ship into generated projects during tests. Generation stamps the newest eligible uv (ADR-0008), which the ambient uv in CI cannot satisfy, so every matrix cell failed on the version mismatch. And a freshly generated project is a day-one project: the scaffold keeps coverage at 100% and the ratchet dormant, and there is no remote for the badge, so the four knob cells never exercised the ratchet, the coverage union, the badge slug or the dependency audit. Decision The snapshot is what git add -A would commit: tracked files plus untracked ones git ignores nothing of, minus deleted ones. Uncommitted edits are tested; ignored files stay out. TEMPLATE_UV_VERSION pins what generation stamps to the template's committed pin, read from the template source so it follows maintain.bump-uv . The matrix is the cartesian product of host and Pages, four cells, plus one matured cell: a GitHub project with the smoke test replaced by one that leaves an import uncalled, a version-gated module so the union exceeds any single interpreter, and an origin remote. The dependency audit rides with that cell only, so a transient advisory-service error fails one job instead of five. Each cell runs preflight --write , then the bare preflight to prove the tree it wrote passes the read-only gate, then checks that nothing was left untracked. test.matrix is sequential by default; CI fans the cells out across runners instead. Consequences Four entry points, fastest first: test.invariants , test , test.combo , test.matrix . The matured cell is one extra cell rather than a third axis, because nothing it touches interacts with the knobs. The litter check lives here and not in generated projects, because it is only sound on a freshly generated, fully committed tree. References Commits 64f75a5 (matrix), 6cf4733 ( TEMPLATE_UV_VERSION ), 16251c1 (matured cell), f73f484 (audit in one cell), 5295804 (snapshot). Test the template .

docs.text: ADR-0040: The default branch is a copier answer Status : accepted Date : 2026-11-12 Context ADR-0014 made the version bump arriving on the default branch what a release is. That gave the branch's name a job in five places: the publish workflow's trigger, the Pages workflow's trigger, the check in release that refuses to start anywhere else, the base of the release pull or merge request, and the CI badge, which reads the status of one named branch. All five spelled main , and ADR-0014 closed by noting it. A project whose default branch is not main therefore had every one of them wrong, and a copier update put them back. The GitLab pipeline was the exception: GitLab names the branch itself as $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH , so that rule needed no spelling. GitHub Actions has no such variable in a trigger, since on.push.branches is read before any job runs, which rules out computing the name at run time. Decision default_branch is a copier question, default main . The validator takes what git check-ref-format --branch would, narrowed to the characters that need no quoting in a YAML list or a badge URL: letters, digits, . , _ , / and - , starting with a letter or digit, no .. , not ending in / or .lock . The answer is spelled in one place at run time, DEFAULT_BRANCH in _CI/tasks/configuration.py , which release , the host modules' badge and pull-request helpers read. The two workflow files have it rendered in at generation, because a trigger cannot read a module. pages.yaml became a .jinja file for that, with its Actions expressions inside {% raw %} blocks as publish.yaml already had. The GitLab pipeline keeps $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH ; the answer has to agree with the project's setting there, which the question's help says. Prose that named the branch now either renders the answer, in the pages copier renders, or says "the default branch", in the pages it copies verbatim. The template's own tests generate the matrix cells with the default and one extra project with trunk , then search that project for the word main . A cell generated with the default cannot tell a rendered answer from a literal left behind. Consequences Renaming the default branch is a copier update with a new answer. Existing projects are asked once and keep main by accepting the default. Where the name is spelled is now a property the invariant suite enforces, so a future task or workflow that writes main fails the test rather than waiting for a project on another branch to find it. The branch is still one name for the whole project. A project that releases from several branches is outside what the template describes, as before. pages.yaml is a template now, so an edit to it has to keep every ${{ }} inside a raw block or generation fails on the first one copier tries to render. References ADR-0014 , which named this as the next decision in its area. Copier questions: default_branch .

The validator takes what git check-ref-format --branch would, narrowed to the characters that need no quoting in a YAML list or a badge URL: letters, digits, . , _ , / and - , starting with a letter or digit, no .. , not ending in / or .lock . The answer is spelled in one place at run time, DEFAULT_BRANCH in _CI/tasks/configuration.py , which release , the host modules' badge and pull-request helpers read. The two workflow files have it rendered in at generation, because a trigger cannot read a module. pages.yaml became a .jinja file for that, with its Actions expressions inside {% raw %} blocks as publish.yaml already had. The GitLab pipeline keeps $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH ; the answer has to agree with the project's setting there, which the question's help says. Prose that named the branch now either renders the answer, in the pages copier renders, or says "the default branch", in the pages it copies verbatim. The template's own tests generate the matrix cells with the default and one extra project with trunk , then search that project for the word main . A cell generated with the default cannot tell a rendered answer from a literal left behind.
docs.title: Decision

docs.text: Renaming the default branch is a copier update with a new answer. Existing projects are asked once and keep main by accepting the default. Where the name is spelled is now a property the invariant suite enforces, so a future task or workflow that writes main fails the test rather than waiting for a project on another branch to find it. The branch is still one name for the whole project. A project that releases from several branches is outside what the template describes, as before. pages.yaml is a template now, so an edit to it has to keep every ${{ }} inside a raw block or generation fails on the first one copier tries to render.

docs.text: Design principles The template is opinionated. The choices below were made deliberately, not by accumulation — each replaces something an earlier revision relied on. This page is the overview; each principle has a dated decision record with the situation it was made in and what it cost. Pipelines run template commands only Records: ADR-0004 , ADR-0033 , ADR-0034 , ADR-0035 , ADR-0036 . Every CI step is a ./workflow.cmd <task> call — no inline uv … , pip install … , ad-hoc properdocs … , or other business logic in YAML. Behaviour changes happen in _CI/tasks/ ; workflow files are glue. Two side-effects of this rule earn the rule a section of its own: Parity. What CI runs is exactly what you can run locally. Debugging a failing CI step means running the same ./workflow.cmd command on your laptop. No "but it worked on my machine" gap, no separate path to maintain. And those commands lean on tracked dependencies. When a properdocs / uv / pytest invocation can do a CI step, we prefer it over a GitHub Action, because every Python dependency is pinned in uv.lock and surfaces in the project SBOM. Action dependencies are hidden inside uses: references and never appear in the supply-chain picture. Concretely: properdocs gh-deploy over actions/upload-pages-artifact + actions/deploy-pages ; ./workflow.cmd test over inline pytest invocations; and so on. Three actions are unavoidable: actions/checkout to fetch the repo, astral-sh/setup-uv to bootstrap the toolchain itself when the deps image isn't used, and actions/attest-build-provenance , since GitHub's own provenance attestation can only be recorded by GitHub — beyond those, prefer commands. The QA gate Records: ADR-0009 , ADR-0010 , ADR-0011 , ADR-0022 , ADR-0023 , ADR-0024 , ADR-0026 , ADR-0027 . The QA gate is not a command; it is the role a command plays. preflight with no flags is the gate: it runs every check, compares every derived value against what the tools just measured, writes nothing, and exits non-zero if anything is wrong or out of date. "The gate" is the short form used from here on; the individual tools it runs — format , lint , test , quality , build — are the QA checks. That is what the pre-push hook runs and what the CI pipeline runs, character for character. The commit hook runs the part of the same declaration that can be judged from the files you staged. Give preflight the --write flag and it stops being a gate: the same steps run, but the derived files are updated instead of compared. Eight rules hold this together, and they fall into two kinds. The first kind is about how the checks run. The second is about who may write the values the checks later compare — which belongs here because it is what makes comparing meaningful: a gate can only hold a badge to a measurement if exactly one thing ever writes that badge, and only from a run that measured it. How the checks run One registry, three consumers. STEPS in _CI/tasks/preflight.py declares every check once, with its scope, its path filter and whether it writes. The commit hook, the pre-push hook and the CI job read that declaration rather than keeping their own lists, so a check added there reaches all three without editing three files — and two lists of checks can never disagree about what "green" means. Scope decides the tier. A check that answers correctly from the staged files alone runs on every commit; one that needs the whole program runs on push. ty needs the callers of a changed signature, pyscn needs every file to know what is dead or duplicated, the matrix needs the suite on every interpreter, and a wheel builds from the whole tree or not at all. This is a rule about correctness rather than speed: a whole-program check narrowed to a diff does not run faster, it answers wrongly. One run reports everything you must fix. Steps keep running after one fails, and the run exits non-zero at the end. A gate that stops at the first failure makes you re-run to discover the second, and the steps are ordered cheapest-first so the verdict itself is early even when the run is not. The gate produces what the gate consumes. Every report a gate run writes has a reader inside that run — the coverage JSON the badge reads, the pyscn JSON the grade comes from. Nothing renders a browsable HTML report that no hook and no pipeline opens; test.coverage and quality.pyscn-analyze produce those on demand, for a human who asked. Who may write what the checks measure Verifying is the default; writing is a flag. The bare command compares; --write updates. So the gate needs no flag, and reproducing a pipeline failure means typing what you see in the log. The general form is about names: a command named for an inspection may not modify the tree, and one named for a mutation may — which is why format and release.bump write without being asked and nothing else does. A derived value is written by whatever measured it. The coverage badge is written by the command that ran the matrix, the pyscn badge by the command that produced the grade, the version badge by the command that bumps the version. No task refreshes a value it did not compute, because a value copied from a report nobody just produced is a claim about a tree that may no longer exist. A name carries a scope. reports/coverage.json means coverage across every interpreter in env_list ; reports/coverage.py311.json means one of them; coverage.local.json means whichever one a bare pytest happened to use. Whatever writes one of those names has to be running at that scope, because the readers cannot tell — the badge and the ratchet read a filename, not a provenance. Flags add; they never subtract. The bare command is the narrow, read-only one: --write updates derived files, --audit-dependencies adds a step. No flag makes a gate check less, a gate you can quietly weaken being one that stops meaning anything. env_list in pyproject.toml is what shortens the test matrix, and it shortens CI with it. One consequence of the two kinds meeting: the derived-value steps are skipped once anything has failed, in either mode. A badge computed from a tree that just failed its checks asserts something untrue about it, so there is nothing for --write to write and nothing for the gate to compare. Together these are what make one command mean the same thing in three places. uv is the only tool you install Records: ADR-0002 , ADR-0008 . Earlier revisions asked users to install Python, then pipx , then tox , then pre-commit , then commitizen . Today, every one of those is a uv-managed dependency group inside the generated project. You install uv; uv installs the rest. Tradeoff: the template is now bound to uv's lifecycle. If uv goes away or changes lock format incompatibly, the template needs work. We accept that risk because uv has compressed the toolchain to a single binary that's fast enough to run on every commit. Why groups, not extras Record: ADR-0005 . The template used to put dev tools under [project.optional-dependencies] (PEP 621 extras). Those work but they conflate two ideas: Optional features of the library (e.g. an excel extra for openpyxl support). Internal dev concerns (lint, test, docs). PEP 735 dependency groups — uv's first-class support for them — are explicitly for the second category. They never ship in the wheel and are never user-installable via pip install <pkg>[<extra>] . Cleaner contract, less to explain to users. Ruff replaces Black + isort + flake8 (and most of pylint) Record: ADR-0016 . One tool, one config block, one cache. Ruff doesn't yet cover everything pylint does — so pylint stays, but only for the checks Ruff doesn't have. We expect pylint's role to shrink as Ruff grows. ty replaces mypy Record: ADR-0017 . ty is Astral's type checker, written in Rust. It's faster than mypy and shares the Ruff/uv codebase's quality bar. Mypy compatibility issues still surface occasionally; we accept that trade for the speed and consistency. pytest, not unittest Records: ADR-0018 , ADR-0025 . The original lineage used python -m unittest . We moved to pytest for fixtures, parametrization, coverage integration, and parallel execution via xdist. Unittest test classes still work — pytest discovers them. Conventional Commits drive the release notes Records: ADR-0019 , ADR-0014 for how a release reaches the default branch, and ADR-0040 for where that branch's name comes from. Commit messages must follow Conventional Commits — the lint step rejects anything that doesn't parse. We use them for automatic release notes : commitizen reads the commits since the last tag and groups them by prefix ( feat: , fix: , etc.) into a generated changelog. We do not use commitizen's autorelease mode. The version bump is an explicit choice you make at release time: ./workflow.cmd release -i <major|minor|patch|…> . Commit prefixes inform changelog structure, not the version number. properdocs (not vanilla mkdocs), with mkdocstrings for API docs Records: ADR-0020 , ADR-0037 . properdocs is mkdocs with a curated plugin set. mkdocstrings reads the source directly — no .rst files in the middle. Sphinx is more capable; we don't need that capability here. SBOMs ship inside the wheel Records: ADR-0012 , ADR-0013 , ADR-0021 , ADR-0028 , ADR-0029 , ADR-0032 . Every release composes a CycloneDX 1.7 SBOM covering four sources — runtime dependencies (from uv export --no-dev against the lockfile), dev / build / develop / lint / test / docs / quality / security groups (the lockfile minus the runtime set), vendored CI tooling (every package in _CI/lib/vendor.txt ), and the chosen host's pipeline components (GitHub Actions uses: refs or GitLab CI image: refs). Each component carries an SPDX-identified licence, a SHA-256 hash where the lockfile provides one, and an external_reference pointing at its upstream page. CycloneDX scope ( required / optional / excluded ) distinguishes what ships in the wheel from what builds it. A two-level dependency graph (project → runtime + dev + a synthetic build-environment → vendored + pipeline) makes "what's in the wheel" vs "what built the wheel" walkable from the root bom-ref. The SBOM is validated against the CycloneDX 1.7 JSON schema and written to src/<project_slug>/sbom.cdx.json , which uv build automatically ships inside the wheel rather than next to it. A downstream consumer extracts it with unzip -p <wheel> <project_slug>/sbom.cdx.json or importlib.resources — the SBOM travels with the artefact instead of needing to be re-correlated post-release. The cost is one Python module ( _CI/tasks/sbom.py ) and one extra build step; the benefit is that supply-chain questions have an answer the day someone asks them, without depending on a separate registry or pinned cyclonedx-cli binary. Vendored CI tooling Records: ADR-0003 , ADR-0015 . _CI/lib/vendor/ ships Invoke + its dependencies committed to the repo. ./workflow.cmd works on a fresh clone with only uv installed — no pip install invoke step, no version drift between contributor machines. The vendoring cost is bytes in the repo; the benefit is that the dev cycle is the same on day one as on day one thousand. Diátaxis for our own docs Record: ADR-0007 . The four sections — Tutorials, How-to, Reference, Explanation — exist because the template's documentation has historically conflated "I want to start" with "I want to understand", and readers got annoyed at both. Diátaxis splits the audiences. This page is in Explanation because it tells you why ; it won't show you how to change anything. What we deliberately do not do Record: ADR-0006 . No framework choice. This is a library scaffold. It does not know about FastAPI, Django, or Click. Add what you need. No monorepo support. One package, one repo. If you want a monorepo, use a different template. No Python below the project's chosen min_python_version (as low as 3.11). tomllib is in the standard library from 3.11, the template's floor, so no fallback is needed. No GitHub-only or GitLab-only assumptions in the dev cycle. Host-specific code lives in _CI/tasks/<host>.py ; the rest of the workflow runs identically. See also Why copier? — why we picked the template format we did. History and lineage — what this template was forked from and why.
