docs.text: Publish docs to GitHub Pages For GitHub-hosted projects, the template ships .github/workflows/pages.yaml by default. It runs ./workflow.cmd document.deploy-github when a release lands on the default branch, which delegates to properdocs gh-deploy (no GitHub Pages deploy actions involved — see Design principles for the reasoning). The only manual step is enabling Pages on the GitHub side. The Pages scaffolding is opt-in/opt-out at generation time via the integrate_pages question (default true ). Answering false omits both the workflow file and the matching document.deploy-github task from the generated project — see Copier questions . Step 1 — Push the template Generate the project with git_hosting_service=github , push to GitHub. The workflow creates the gh-pages branch on its first successful run — which happens on your first release, or immediately if you trigger it by hand from the Actions tab ( workflow_dispatch ), which is how a project that has not released yet gets a site. Step 2 — Enable Pages on the repo On GitHub: Settings → Pages . Source : Deploy from a branch . Branch : gh-pages / / (root) . The branch only appears after the first workflow run completes — wait for the Actions tab to show a green Pages run, then configure. That's it. Each subsequent release redeploys automatically. The site lives at https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/ . Why gh-pages branch instead of the Actions-source flow? Two related design principles drive this choice: Pipelines run template commands only. The workflow's only substantive step is ./workflow.cmd document.deploy-github . Every behaviour change happens in _CI/tasks/document.py , not in the YAML. Track every dependency in the SBOM. properdocs gh-deploy is a Python command resolved from the locked document dependency group. actions/upload-pages-artifact and actions/deploy-pages would bring transitive dependencies that don't appear in uv.lock or the CycloneDX SBOM. Avoiding them keeps the supply-chain story honest. See Design principles . About the Node.js deprecation warning After each deploy you may see a deprecation warning on the pages build and deployment workflow run — not on our Pages workflow. The warning reads: Node.js 20 actions are deprecated. The following actions are running on Node.js 20 and may not work as expected: actions/checkout@v4, actions/upload-artifact@v4. That run is a GitHub-managed pipeline ( dynamic/pages/pages-build-deployment ) that the platform auto-triggers whenever the gh-pages branch updates. It is not defined in .github/workflows/ and we cannot edit it. The deprecated actions/checkout@v4 and actions/upload-artifact@v4 references live inside that internal pipeline, not in our own workflow files — every action we do control is already pinned to its latest immutable release. The warning is expected and intentionally not addressed. Silencing it would require switching to the actions/upload-pages-artifact + actions/deploy-pages flow, which would violate both design principles above. We accept the warning as the cost of keeping deploy logic in _CI/tasks/document.py and outside the SBOM-tracked dependency surface. GitHub will update their internal pipeline on their own timeline. Concurrency The workflow uses concurrency: { group: pages, cancel-in-progress: false } . If you push twice in quick succession, the second deploy waits for the first to finish rather than racing it. Cancelling mid-deploy would leave the gh-pages branch in an indeterminate state. Why on release rather than on every push Docs built from the default branch describe code that is in no release yet, so a reader following them can reach for a function they cannot install. The workflow triggers on a push to that branch and asks ./workflow.cmd release.detect whether it carried a release — a change of [project].version — the same question publish.yaml asks through release.ship , so the site and the package cannot disagree about what counts as released. Not a push: tags: ['v*'] trigger: ./workflow.cmd release creates no tag. The publish job creates it on the default branch once the release has merged, which is after the docs should go out. A site tracking the default branch as well means versioned docs — a stable build plus a dev one — rather than a trigger change, which is more machinery than the template ships today. Custom domain After the first deploy: Add a CNAME file containing your domain to the docs/ directory. Configure DNS — ALIAS/ANAME for an apex domain, CNAME for a subdomain — pointing at <owner>.github.io . Settings → Pages → Custom domain to set it on the GitHub side. The next release redeploys with the custom domain (or trigger the workflow by hand). GitLab Pages instead For GitLab-hosted projects, the equivalent is a pages: job in .gitlab-ci.yml that publishes the site/ directory. The template doesn't ship one yet — it's the logical follow-up to this workflow. See also The shipped workflows — pages.yaml lives under the conditionally named .github/workflows/ directory; the YAML is kept short on purpose. Design principles — the two rules behind the workflow's shape.

docs.text: Update an existing project with copier When this template ships a new version, you can pull the changes into an existing generated project without re-generating from scratch. copier records the template revision your project was generated from — it's stored in .copier-answers.yml — and produces a reviewable diff against the latest version. The basic update From the root of your generated project: uvx copier update --trust --trust is required because the template runs a post-copy task ( tasks_render.py ). Copier will not execute tasks from a template it doesn't trust. copier: Re-renders the template at the new revision using your stored answers ( .copier-answers.yml ). Performs a three-way merge against your current files. Applies the result, flagging conflicts for manual resolution. Review the changes with git diff , run ./workflow.cmd format && ./workflow.cmd preflight , and commit when happy. When questions have changed If the new template version added or renamed a question (for example git_hosting_service was added in an earlier revision), copier will prompt for any missing answers during the update. Provide them — your .copier-answers.yml is updated in place. Upgrading past the Dependency-Track removal Earlier versions asked integrate_dependency_track and, when it was on, uploaded the SBOM to an OWASP Dependency-Track server after every publish. The template no longer does this. The SBOM is still generated, validated and shipped inside every wheel. Only the upload is gone. Updating removes: the secure.sbom-upload task and the OWASP_DTRACK_SETTINGS constant in _CI/tasks/configuration.py ; the OWASP_DTRACK_URL / OWASP_DTRACK_API_KEY environment block in the GitHub publish workflow; the Upload an SBOM to Dependency Track page from the developer docs. Copier no longer asks the question, and an integrate_dependency_track line left in .copier-answers.yml has no effect. If you customised any of the removed code, expect conflicts in secure.py , release.py or publish.yaml . Resolve them in favour of the template's version. After the update: Delete the OWASP_DTRACK_URL and OWASP_DTRACK_API_KEY secrets from your repository or group CI settings. Nothing reads them any more. If your organisation still wants every release in Dependency-Track, add the upload as your own task in _CI/tasks/local.py , which copier update never touches (see Add a workflow task in your project's developer docs), and call it from your pipeline after release.publish . The SBOM to send is src/<your_package>/sbom.cdx.json . Dependency-Track's CI/CD integration guide documents the upload endpoint. Upgrading past the packaging-conformance change This change adds a question and three checks: repository_url is asked once. Answer it to get [project.urls] (PyPI's sidebar links); leave it empty to skip. New gates. lint.pyproject (validate-pyproject) runs on commits that stage pyproject.toml and in preflight ; build.package now runs twine check --strict and check-wheel-contents . A pyproject.toml you edited may fail the first run. The error names the field; fix it rather than skip the gate. New dependency group build , and new pins in lint and security . Run uv lock after the update and commit uv.lock with it. Publishing. The publish job now signs PEP 740 attestations. On GitLab it also requests id_tokens: , and PyPI needs a Trusted Publisher registered for the project (the new Set up Trusted Publishing how-to). If you publish with UV_PUBLISH_* credentials, nothing changes: that path uploads without attestations. Upgrading past the default-branch question copier update asks default_branch , with main as the default. Accept it if your default branch is main and nothing changes. Answer with your branch's name otherwise: the publish and Pages workflows start triggering on it, release starts from it, release pull or merge requests target it, and the CI badge reads it. Before the question, all of those spelled main , so a project on another branch had to edit each by hand after every update. See ADR-0040 . Upgrading past the tag-on-main release flow release used to create the tag on the release branch and push it with the branch. On GitLab that published the version before the MR was reviewed; on both hosts a squash merge left the tag pointing at a commit main never saw, and nothing published. Now release creates no tag. The publish job runs on every push to the default branch and hands it to release.ship , which publishes when [project].version changed between the previous tip and the new one: it creates the tag on the new tip through the host's Release API (a Release entry appears on the releases page), then builds, signs and uploads. Merge release PRs/MRs any way you like. Updating changes: .github/workflows/publish.yaml or .gitlab-ci.yml : the publish job runs release.ship and, on GitHub, holds contents: write so GITHUB_TOKEN can create the tag. detect-release-tag.yaml is gone; pages.yaml runs release.detect itself. release.bump commits the version files itself; release.changelog takes --version ; release.push , which had become a bare git push once tags were CI's to create, is gone. After the update: If the pypi environment has required reviewers or approvers, remove them and restrict the environment to the default branch instead; the job now runs on every push to it. The PyPI Trusted Publisher registration itself is unchanged. On GitHub, if a ruleset restricts who may create v* tags, add a bypass for GitHub Actions, or release.tag fails. A release branch opened before the update carries a tag on its bump commit. Delete that tag everywhere ( git tag -d vX.Y.Z && git push origin :refs/tags/vX.Y.Z ) before merging, or release.tag refuses to create it on the default branch because it exists on another commit. Upgrading past the changelog move Releases used to write the changelog to docs/changelog.md , a page missing from the docs nav, while Reference → Changelog showed a placeholder that never changed. They now write docs/reference/changelog.md , the page the nav shows. Nothing is lost: the new page has no releases in it yet, so the first release.changelog after the update writes your full history into it from the tags, below the page's header. Later releases add their entries on top. Delete docs/changelog.md in that release, or any time after. If you hand-edited entries there, copy them across before deleting it, since the history is rebuilt from commit messages. Resolving conflicts Copier uses a three-way merge; conflicts appear as standard conflict markers in the affected files. The most common cause is that you customised a file the template also changed. Resolve them by hand and re-run ./workflow.cmd test . Pinning a specific template version By default copier update fetches the latest tagged release. To pin to a specific ref: uvx copier update --trust --vcs-ref <tag-or-commit> When the upstream is unreachable copier update needs network access to fetch the template. In an air-gapped environment, clone the template repo separately and point copier at the local path: uvx copier update --trust /path/to/local/clone See also Copier documentation — the full update workflow. Copier questions — what each answer in .copier-answers.yml controls.

After the update: Delete the OWASP_DTRACK_URL and OWASP_DTRACK_API_KEY secrets from your repository or group CI settings. Nothing reads them any more. If your organisation still wants every release in Dependency-Track, add the upload as your own task in _CI/tasks/local.py , which copier update never touches (see Add a workflow task in your project's developer docs), and call it from your pipeline after release.publish . The SBOM to send is src/<your_package>/sbom.cdx.json . Dependency-Track's CI/CD integration guide documents the upload endpoint.
docs.title: Upgrading past the Dependency-Track removal

docs.text: This change adds a question and three checks: repository_url is asked once. Answer it to get [project.urls] (PyPI's sidebar links); leave it empty to skip. New gates. lint.pyproject (validate-pyproject) runs on commits that stage pyproject.toml and in preflight ; build.package now runs twine check --strict and check-wheel-contents . A pyproject.toml you edited may fail the first run. The error names the field; fix it rather than skip the gate. New dependency group build , and new pins in lint and security . Run uv lock after the update and commit uv.lock with it. Publishing. The publish job now signs PEP 740 attestations. On GitLab it also requests id_tokens: , and PyPI needs a Trusted Publisher registered for the project (the new Set up Trusted Publishing how-to). If you publish with UV_PUBLISH_* credentials, nothing changes: that path uploads without attestations.
docs.title: Upgrading past the packaging-conformance change

docs.text: copier update asks default_branch , with main as the default. Accept it if your default branch is main and nothing changes. Answer with your branch's name otherwise: the publish and Pages workflows start triggering on it, release starts from it, release pull or merge requests target it, and the CI badge reads it. Before the question, all of those spelled main , so a project on another branch had to edit each by hand after every update. See ADR-0040 .
docs.title: Upgrading past the default-branch question

docs.text: release used to create the tag on the release branch and push it with the branch. On GitLab that published the version before the MR was reviewed; on both hosts a squash merge left the tag pointing at a commit main never saw, and nothing published. Now release creates no tag. The publish job runs on every push to the default branch and hands it to release.ship , which publishes when [project].version changed between the previous tip and the new one: it creates the tag on the new tip through the host's Release API (a Release entry appears on the releases page), then builds, signs and uploads. Merge release PRs/MRs any way you like. Updating changes: .github/workflows/publish.yaml or .gitlab-ci.yml : the publish job runs release.ship and, on GitHub, holds contents: write so GITHUB_TOKEN can create the tag. detect-release-tag.yaml is gone; pages.yaml runs release.detect itself. release.bump commits the version files itself; release.changelog takes --version ; release.push , which had become a bare git push once tags were CI's to create, is gone. After the update: If the pypi environment has required reviewers or approvers, remove them and restrict the environment to the default branch instead; the job now runs on every push to it. The PyPI Trusted Publisher registration itself is unchanged. On GitHub, if a ruleset restricts who may create v* tags, add a bypass for GitHub Actions, or release.tag fails. A release branch opened before the update carries a tag on its bump commit. Delete that tag everywhere ( git tag -d vX.Y.Z && git push origin :refs/tags/vX.Y.Z ) before merging, or release.tag refuses to create it on the default branch because it exists on another commit.
docs.title: Upgrading past the tag-on-main release flow

docs.text: Releases used to write the changelog to docs/changelog.md , a page missing from the docs nav, while Reference → Changelog showed a placeholder that never changed. They now write docs/reference/changelog.md , the page the nav shows. Nothing is lost: the new page has no releases in it yet, so the first release.changelog after the update writes your full history into it from the tags, below the page's header. Later releases add their entries on top. Delete docs/changelog.md in that release, or any time after. If you hand-edited entries there, copy them across before deleting it, since the history is rebuilt from commit messages.
docs.title: Upgrading past the changelog move

docs.text: Copier uses a three-way merge; conflicts appear as standard conflict markers in the affected files. The most common cause is that you customised a file the template also changed. Resolve them by hand and re-run ./workflow.cmd test .
docs.title: Resolving conflicts

docs.text: By default copier update fetches the latest tagged release. To pin to a specific ref: uvx copier update --trust --vcs-ref <tag-or-commit>
docs.title: Pinning a specific template version

docs.text: copier update needs network access to fetch the template. In an air-gapped environment, clone the template repo separately and point copier at the local path: uvx copier update --trust /path/to/local/clone

docs.text: Copier questions Every question in copier.yml , what it does, and how it's validated. The template config file is copier.yml at the repo root; the tool you invoke is copier. User-facing questions project_name Type : string Default : Paleofuturistic Python Project Human-readable name. Appears as the README title and the docs site_name ; pyproject.toml 's name is project_slug . project_slug Type : string (prompted, pre-filled with a derived default you can accept or edit) Default : project_name lowercased, with every run of non-identifier characters replaced by a single underscore and leading/trailing underscores stripped — e.g. Username's Toolkit → username_s_toolkit . Python package name: both the import name / source-tree directory ( src/<slug>/ ) and the pyproject.toml distribution name. It must therefore be a valid Python identifier and a valid PyPI project name : lowercase ASCII letters, digits, and underscores, starting with a letter and ending with a letter or digit. A validator on this question enforces exactly that — it re-prompts (or, in non-interactive runs, aborts) on an empty value, a leading digit, or leftover punctuation such as an apostrophe. Because PyPI normalizes names — lowercasing and collapsing runs of . , - , or _ to a single - — the distribution name and the import name legitimately differ: username_s_toolkit is published and installed as username-s-toolkit ( pip install username-s-toolkit ) but imported as import username_s_toolkit . project_description Type : string Default : Development flow as Paleofuturistic Python One-line summary. Lands in pyproject.toml 's description and the README lead paragraph. full_name Type : string Default : John Doe Author name. Appears in pyproject.toml authors metadata and the chosen LICENSE file. email Type : string Default : me@here.now Author email. Appears in pyproject.toml authors metadata. min_python_version Type : choice Default : 3.11 Allowed : "3.11" , "3.12" , "3.13" , "3.14" , "3.15" Lower bound. Drives requires-python , classifier list, tox envs, and CI matrix. See Choose the Python version range . max_python_version Type : choice Default : 3.15 Allowed : "3.11" , "3.12" , "3.13" , "3.14" , "3.15" Upper bound. Must be >= min_python_version and share the same major version. A validator on this question in copier.yml enforces both constraints at generation time and aborts with a clear error if they are violated. license Type : choice Default : Apache-2.0 Allowed : Apache-2.0 , MIT , BSD-3-Clause , None Selects which license file is installed to LICENSE by tasks_render.py . See License options . git_hosting_service Type : choice Default : github Allowed : github , gitlab Determines which CI scaffolding ships and which host-specific submodule lives at _CI/tasks/<host>.py . The unchosen host's files are omitted at generation time via copier conditional filenames — a file or directory whose rendered name is an empty string is simply not created. See Choose a git host . default_branch Type : string Default : main Allowed : a branch name git accepts, without characters that would need quoting in YAML or a URL: letters, digits, . , _ , / and - , starting with a letter or digit, no .. , not ending in / or .lock The branch releases land on. The publish workflow or pipeline triggers on it by name, the Pages workflow does too, release refuses to start from any other branch, the release pull or merge request targets it, and the CI badge reads its status. The tasks read it from DEFAULT_BRANCH in _CI/tasks/configuration.py ; the workflow files have it written in at generation time, since a trigger cannot be computed at run time. Renaming the branch later is a copier update with a new answer. On GitLab the answer has to match the project's default branch setting, which .gitlab-ci.yml reads as $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH . See ADR-0040 . repository_url Type : string Default : empty Allowed : empty, or an https:// URL with a path, e.g. https://github.com/acme/widget The public home of the repository. It renders [project.urls] in pyproject.toml , the links PyPI shows in the project sidebar, under well-known labels so each gets its own icon: Label Value Homepage The GitHub Pages site when git_hosting_service=github , the repository is on github.com and integrate_pages=true ; otherwise the repository Source The repository Issues <repository>/issues on GitHub, <repository>/-/issues on GitLab Changelog docs/reference/changelog.md on the default branch, the page release updates Documentation The GitHub Pages site, under the same conditions as Homepage A trailing / or .git is dropped, so a pasted clone URL works. Left empty, the project ships no [project.urls] at all rather than links that would 404 on PyPI; answer it on a later copier update , or add the table by hand. Self-hosted GitLab and GitHub Enterprise URLs work too; only the Pages links assume github.com. integrate_pages Type : bool Default : true Asked when : git_hosting_service=github Controls whether documentation-publishing scaffolding (the Pages workflow file and the matching document.deploy-github task) ships in the generated project. The scaffolding is GitHub-specific, so GitLab projects are not asked; the answer keeps its default there and nothing reads it. See Publish docs to GitHub Pages . Validation Validation is split between copier's built-in mechanisms and the tasks_render.py copy-time script: Python version range — a validator on the max_python_version question in copier.yml checks that max >= min , that both values share the same major version, and that both appear in the choices list. Any failure aborts generation immediately before any files are written. Project slug — a validator on the project_slug question checks the value is a valid Python identifier and PyPI project name ( ^[a-z]([a-z0-9_]*[a-z0-9])?$ ), rejecting empty values, leading digits, and punctuation such as apostrophes. Generation aborts before any files are written on failure. Repository URL — a validator on repository_url accepts an empty value or ^https://[^/\s]+/[^\s]+$ , so http:// , SSH remotes and a bare host are refused before any files are written. Default branch — a validator on default_branch refuses an empty value and the names git check-ref-format --branch would refuse that the pattern can express: a leading - or . , .. , a trailing / or .lock , and any character outside letters, digits, . , _ , / and - . License installation — tasks_render.py installs the chosen LICENSE file (substituting author/year tokens) and removes the licenses/ staging directory. It runs only on copier copy , not on copier update . See also Generation internals — what runs after these answers are collected. Generated project tree — what each answer ends up shaping in the output.

docs.text: License options The questionnaire's license answer picks one of four entries. Each maps to a file shipped to LICENSE . No license header or metadata is added to individual source files. Choice SPDX ID Notes Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 Default. Permissive, includes explicit patent grant. MIT MIT Permissive, minimal. BSD-3-Clause BSD-3-Clause Permissive, includes attribution clause. None — No LICENSE file. Useful for proprietary code or when you'll add a license later. What tasks_render.py does with each For non- None choices, tasks_render.py at copy time: Copies licenses/<choice> to LICENSE in the project root, interpolating {year} (current calendar year) and {author} from full_name . Then it deletes the licenses/ directory regardless of choice. For None , only the directory cleanup runs — no LICENSE file is written. Picking later License: None at generation time, then deciding later: Add a LICENSE file at the project root. Set pyproject.toml 's license = "<SPDX-ID>" and license-files = ["LICENSE"] , the two fields a generated project ships when a licence was chosen. PyPI classifiers If you want PyPI to display a license badge, add the matching classifier to pyproject.toml 's [project] classifiers list. Recognized strings are listed at pypi.org/classifiers/ — look under License :: OSI Approved . The template doesn't auto-add classifiers because they're orthogonal to the license metadata field and not all licenses have a classifier.

docs.text: From zero to a published package This tutorial picks up where Generate your first project left off: a freshly generated project with a green dev cycle. We'll make a real change, cut a release, and publish to PyPI. You'll need a PyPI account and a public git remote before the publish step. Step 1 — Write a feature Open src/<your_project_slug>/<your_project_slug>.py and replace the body of hello() with something more interesting, for example: def hello(greeting: str = 'Hello', someone: str = 'you') -> str: """Greet someone. Args: greeting: The greeting message. someone: The name of the person to greet. Returns: A greeting message. """ return f'{greeting} {someone} from test_260708!' Update the smoke test under tests/ to match if needed. Commit: git add -A git commit -m "feat: greet someone with a specific word" Reminders: All relevant checks for pre-commit run on staged files (Ruff format/check, validate-pyproject, pylint, complexipy, conventional commit messages). Commit messages drive the release notes, not the version bump. Step 2 — Integrate For this tutorial we will assume you use GitHub as your git remote. Create a repository on GitHub. It must be public if you want to publish public GH pages, as we do at the end of this tutorial. Do not add any files like README, LICENSE etc. Run the following commands in your project directory to connect to the remote (replace your_handle / test_260708 with your git remote handle / project name here and in the following examples): git remote add origin git@github.com:your_handle/test_260708.git ./workflow.cmd preflight --write git add README.md git commit -m "docs: point the build badge at the repository" git push -u origin main Preflight might fail if you did some more exotic edits than the example above. Don't worry. It will tell you what to fix; do that, commit and then try to push all. Note that preflight also runs as a QA gate before actually pushing. The first preflight wrote the build badge to your README. It could not be written before now, because it's built from git remote get-url origin . This is the one badge you fill in 'by hand', once. The four others — version, Python, coverage and pyscn — are measured from your project, so preflight --write has been keeping them current since the first tutorial. Go to your git remote. A couple of pipelines will have started running. For now only Continuous Integration is the interesting one. It runs the same preflight as before, this time where everyone can see its outcome. Step 3 — Cut the release ./workflow.cmd release -i minor The -i minor is your explicit choice. Valid values: major , minor , patch , alpha , beta , rc . This task: Validates the working tree is clean and synched with origin. Creates a release/<version> branch off main . Bumps the version, writes the changelog, updates the version badge, commits all. Pushes the branch. No tag yet: CI creates vX.Y.Z on main once the release is merged. Opens a release pull request on your git host through its API when a token is set ( GITHUB_TOKEN on GitHub, GITLAB_TOKEN on GitLab), otherwise prints a URL to open it yourself. Note that the security audit pipeline now does run. That is because a commit edited uv.lock . This is a desired side-effect during release. You would not want to release a package with known vulnerabilities (that have not been suppressed in .security-overrides ). Step 4 — Publish to PyPI The publish job builds the wheel and sdist (the SBOM rides inside the wheel), checks both with twine check --strict and check-wheel-contents , signs a PEP 740 attestation per file, and uploads files and attestations together. The recommended path is CI-driven PyPI trusted publishing — no long-lived tokens, and the only way PyPI accepts the attestations. Wire it up once for the project (your generated project's Set up Trusted Publishing how-to has the PyPI form for your host; Harden the GitHub repository covers the GitHub side), then approve and merge the release PR from Step 3, any way you like. The version bump lands on main ; the publish job sees it, creates the tag there, and publishes. After all the pipelines ran you should see your project published on PyPI. Each file's details show a Provenance section naming your repository; if you answered repository_url , the sidebar shows its links. Step 5 — Publish the docs For GitHub-hosted projects, see Publish docs to GitHub Pages for the workflow file and Pages setup. You're done A tagged release exists, a wheel is on PyPI, and your docs are live. Where to go next: Run ./workflow.cmd --list to see all available workflow commands and experiment to create your ideal dev cycle. Look at the (developer) docs in your templated project. It will guide you on practical things, like adding dependencies. Update an existing project with copier — bring future template improvements into this project. Design principles — why the template made the choices it did. When you feel comfortable developing in a project molded by this template activate the test coverage ratchet .

docs.text: Generate your first project This tutorial walks you from an empty directory to a working Python project generated from this template, in about ten minutes. You will not customise anything — the goal is to see the whole cycle once. Prerequisites You need uv installed. uv is the only tool you need; it can run copier for you and will manage every other tool the generated project uses. curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh Step 1 — Generate the project Pick an empty directory and run: uvx copier copy --vcs-ref latest --trust https://github.com/schubergphilis/paleofuturistic_python <destination-dir> --trust is required because the template runs a post-copy task. --vcs-ref is optional, but for stability we recommend only using actual tagged and released versions of this template. You will be asked a series of questions. Press Enter to accept the defaults for every one — they're documented in Copier questions . Three answers worth thinking about: project_name — pick something memorable; everything else is derived. git_hosting_service — github (default) or gitlab ; see Choose a git host . license — defaults to Apache-2.0; pick whatever fits. When the command finishes you'll have a complete Python project inside <destination-dir> . Step 2 — Bootstrap it cd <your-project-slug> git init -b main git add --all git commit -m "chore: initial commit" ./workflow.cmd bootstrap The bootstrap command initialises git if needed and registers the pre-commit hooks (if you select yes, which we highly recommend). Dependencies need no step of their own: every task runs through uv run , which syncs .venv from uv.lock the first time. The command is idempotent — running it again is a no-op until you pass --force . We let you commit the scaffold before bootstrapping, because otherwise the pre-commit hook would validate the whole scaffold. This is time consuming and not necessary, which you can validate by running git status after bootstrapping. Step 3 — Run the QA checks These commands are the heartbeat of every project this template generates: ./workflow.cmd format # format with Ruff (also sort imports, otherwise a normal ruff format) ./workflow.cmd lint # lint with Ruff check, validate-pyproject, pylint, ty (type checker), complexipy, commitizen ./workflow.cmd test # test with pytest (in parallel with xdist using the active Python interpreter) ./workflow.cmd quality # scan code quality with pyscn ./workflow.cmd build # produce a wheel + sdist in dist/ and export an SBOM ./workflow.cmd secure # alert on vulnerable dependencies with pip-audit (also produce an SBOM and lint pip-audit security overrides) You should see a passing test for the example hello() function and a wheel appear under dist/ . Some of the other QA tools also produce output you can look into later. The really fast checks (ruff format/check, validate-pyproject, pylint, complexipy) which can run on only files git-staged are bundled in a one handy command: ./workflow.cmd develop.pre-commit . You are probably not surprised to hear these commands are already set to run before every commit with pre-commit. With the pre-commit check (both CLI and hook) format will not edit your files as it does when you invoke it stand-alone. Your commit message and SBOM security overrides are also checked before landing a commit. Now run: ./workflow.cmd preflight --write This is a more robust check on your project. It will perform all checks above, except for the pip-audit from secure , because that is not related to code changes and does not give deterministic results. (Today's green might be red tomorrow for pip-audit.) If you want those checks as well, then add the flag --audit-dependencies . The --write flag makes the command update the badges in the README.md based on the state of your project. (The README is synched to your docs' index by default.) A fresh project needs the --write on first run to set the badges to a correct value. The default use is without that flag. Then it will fail on stale badges. Next to that, preflight runs pytest over all Python interpreters (with tox) and checks if the documentation renders correctly. Preflight is also the command that executes before making a git push; more on that later. Step 4 — See the docs Run the following command: ./workflow.cmd document A browser tab opens with the generated project's documentation — its own Diátaxis-structured site, ready to extend. The badges should reflect the state of your project if you just ran preflight . (The build badge should still be grey for now, because it will point to the state of your CI/CD system configured later.) Step 5 — Commit using Conventional Commits Commit messages must follow Conventional Commits — the lint step rejects anything that doesn't parse. Start each message with a type prefix: git add -A git commit -m "chore: bootstrap project" Note the relevant checks from pre-commit running before the commit lands. The prefixes drive the release notes : commitizen reads the commit history when generating the changelog and groups your commits by prefix ( feat: under "Features", fix: under "Bug Fixes", etc.). (The prefix does not drive the version bump — you'll choose that explicitly in a later step.) You're done You have a fully scaffolded Python project with tests, linting, packaging, and docs all wired up. Next: From zero to a published package .
